facts.statement: The type specimen of Dyslocosaurus, catalog number AC 663, is housed in the Amherst College Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: The holotype or type specimen the genus is based on, AC 663, is part of the collection of the Amherst College Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: The fossil remains of Dyslocosaurus were collected by Professor Frederic Brewster Loomis.
facts.quote: It was collected by professor Frederic Brewster Loomis.

facts.statement: The only known location for the Dyslocosaurus fossil is Lance Creek, a county in east Wyoming.
facts.quote: However, the only available information regarding its provenance is that given on the label: "Lance Creek", a county in east Wyoming.

facts.statement: John Stanton McIntosh, William Coombs, and Dale Russell described Dyslocosaurus as a new genus and species in 1992.
facts.quote: In 1992, together with William Coombs and Dale Russell, decided to create a new genus and species for it.

facts.statement: The genus name Dyslocosaurus means "hard-to-place lizard" and refers to the scarcity of data about the fossil's original location.
facts.quote: The genus name is derived from Greek dys, "bad, "poor", and Latin locus, "place", a reference to the paucity of data regarding the type locality of the fossil.

facts.statement: The species name polyonychius means "many-clawed" and refers to the unusual number of claws on the foot.
facts.quote: The specific name is derived from Greek polys, "many", and onyx, "claw".

facts.statement: The original describers interpreted the limb bones of Dyslocosaurus as belonging to a diplodocid dinosaur.
facts.quote: The describers interpreted the remains, consisting of some limb bones, as those of a diplodocid dinosaur.

facts.statement: Based on the interpretation of the remains as diplodocid, the describers concluded the animal lived in the Late Jurassic Period.
facts.quote: From this they concluded that it in fact dated from the Late Jurassic Period, like most diplodocids.

facts.statement: Researchers noted that a similar species might have created the Early Cretaceous trackway ichnospecies Brontopodus birdi, which also shows four claws.
facts.quote: A species similar to Dyslocosaurus would have made the tracks of the ichnospecies Brontopodus birdi from the Early Cretaceous, that also features four claws.

facts.statement: In 1998, Paul Sereno and Jeffrey A. Wilson proposed that the Dyslocosaurus specimen was actually a chimera mixing titanosaur limb bones and theropod phalanges from the Lance Formation.
facts.quote: In 1998 Paul Sereno and Jeffrey A. Wilson gave an alternative interpretation: the specimen would come from the Lance Formation after all but be a chimera: in this case a mix up of titanosaur limb bones and theropod phalanges.

facts.statement: In 2015, Tschopp et al. raised doubts about whether Dyslocosaurus had more than three claws, noting that one pedal bone in the specimen differed in preservation and color from the others.
facts.quote: In their taxonomic revision of Diplodocidae, Tschopp et al. in 2015 noted that a pedal phalanx included in AC 663 is apparently not from the same individual as the rest of AC 663 given differences in preservation and coloration among individual bones, raising doubts on whether Dyslocosaurus had more than three claws on the feet.

facts.statement: Some analyses have recovered Dyslocosaurus as a member of the family Dicraeosauridae, potentially making it the second dicraeosaurid known from North America.
facts.quote: Although fragmentary, Dyslocosaurus was recovered as a member of Dicraeosauridae, potentially making it the second record of a dicraeosaurid from North America (the other being Suuwassea).

facts.statement: Dyslocosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic Period, approximately 150 to 147 million years ago, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente 150 y 147 millones de años, en el Kimmeridgiense y el Titoniense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Dyslocosaurus was a sauropod dinosaur similar to Diplodocus but smaller in size.
facts.quote: Dyslocosaurus fue un saurópodo similar al Diplodocus, pero de menor tamaño.

facts.statement: Dyslocosaurus reached lengths of 18 meters, heights of 4.5 meters, and weighed approximately 6 tons.
facts.quote: Alcanzó los 18 metros de largo, 4,5 de alto y un peso de 6 toneladas.

facts.statement: Dyslocosaurus was characterized by having four, possibly five, clawed toes, whereas diplodocids typically have three.
facts.quote: Se caracterizaba por poseer 4 dedos, posiblemente cinco, con garras, mientras que los diplodócidos generalmente tienen tres dedos con garras.

facts.statement: Dyslocosaurus is classified within the family Dicraeosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Dicraeosauridae

facts.statement: Dyslocosaurus belongs to the superfamily Diplodocoidea.
facts.quote: superfamilia: Diplodocoidea

facts.statement: The genus Dyslocosaurus was named by Macintosh, Coombs, and Russell in 1992.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Macintosh, Coombs & Russell, 1992

facts.statement: The time range for Dyslocosaurus is estimated from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Tithonian (154.8 to 143.1 million years ago)
